tier_reason: The vendor benchmark page shows sf1000 total run times for Doris vs ClickHouse (SSB 11.6s vs 82.2s, TPC-H 53.8s vs 279.0s, TPC-DS 173.8s vs 1913.9s), but the SQL-analytics report is marked 'Coming Soon'. No CPU or instance, compiler, or configuration is given, and the repo's tools/ssb-tools, tpch-tools and tpcds-tools scripts run only Doris. That is first-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: sf1000 total run time on the internal-table-format tab: SSB (13 queries) Doris 11.6s vs ClickHouse 82.2s (~7.1x), TPC-H (22 queries) 53.8s vs 279.0s (~5.2x), TPC-DS (99 queries) 173.8s vs 1913.9s (~11.0x) (ratios derived from page data). Redshift and Snowflake are also slower on the page, e.g. SSB 30.1s / 32.9s. Agent-observability tab (100M rows): Analytics Rollups Doris 4.3s vs DuckDB 13485.7s (~3,136x) and Semi-Structured Payload 2.5s vs 17795.2s (~7,118x) (derived from page data). On the same tab ClickHouse takes 42.1s / 42.3s / 24.3s vs Doris 2.3s / 4.3s / 2.5s.
corrections.caveats: This is a vendor page. The SSB/TPC-H/TPC-DS report is 'Coming Soon', and no CPU or instance type, compiler, or engine configuration is stated for those runs. The Doris repo's tools/*-tools scripts cover only Doris, not ClickHouse. The agent-observability numbers come from AgentLogsBench (github.com/velodb/agentlogsbench), published by VeloDB, the company behind Doris, and run on AWS m6i.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 128 GiB) per its blog. Its 3,136x and 7,118x DuckDB multipliers reflect DuckDB's JSON handling collapsing on specific queries, not engine-wide speed. That comparison is also not the ClickHouse baseline this record is about.

notes: The headline ClickHouse numbers match the page exactly. The record's '3,135x' is 13485.7/4.3 ≈ 3,136x, and both DuckDB multipliers are derived, not printed on the page. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 16,005 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-09-26. The Iceberg-format tab is rendered by JS and was not checked.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The paper (arXiv 2603.02001 v2, §5.1) states an AMD EPYC 9654P with 768 GB RAM. The public harness benchmark/run.py with benchmark/systems/duckdb.py and bespoke.py runs against DuckDB. Optimized builds use g++ (the default $CXX) with -std=c++20 -O3 -flto per misc/fasttest/compiler.py and tools/fasttest/run.py. Flags are stated, so the 50x cap does not apply.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-threaded, all systems pinned to the same core with data in memory: TPC-H SF20 total 4.4s vs DuckDB 49.2s (11.17x) and CEB SF2 0.4s vs 19.5s (45.33x). Vs Umbra: 7.24x (TPC-H) and 9.56x (CEB). Per-query vs DuckDB: 2.83x-102x on TPC-H and 11.6x-1500x on CEB. Multi-threaded, 1-64 threads: 7.65x vs DuckDB and 6.12x vs Umbra on TPC-H; 23.97x vs DuckDB and 1.87x vs Umbra on CEB.
corrections.workload: TPC-H (SF20) and CEB, a templated JOB workload on IMDB (SF2, query 8a excluded). An autonomous LLM synthesis pipeline builds a separate workload-specific C++ engine for each benchmark (Bespoke-TPCH, Bespoke-CEB). Headline results compare it single-threaded, pinned to the same core and in memory, against DuckDB 1.4.1 and Umbra 26.02. A 1-64 thread scaling study adds multi-threaded results.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ (default $CXX, version unstated) with -std=c++20 -O3 -flto -fPIC -g for optimized builds (misc/fasttest/compiler.py, tools/fasttest/run.py)
corrections.caveats: The GitHub repo is archived (read-only) and was last pushed 2026-07-22, so it is tagged abandoned. The generated engines are workload-specific (one per benchmark, code in DataManagementLab/BespokeOLAP_Artifacts), not general-purpose. The headline 11.17x and 45.33x figures are single-threaded. DuckDB was not multi-threaded in them, contrary to the original record. CEB Q8a was excluded because of unstable DuckDB runtimes. The compiler version is unstated. The repo harness scripts only the bespoke and duckdb runners, so the Umbra comparison is not scripted. Per-query multipliers up to 1500x reflect workload-specific storage layouts.

notes: The record mislabeled the 11.17x/45.33x figures as multi-threaded; they are single-threaded. The multi-threaded figures are lower (7.65x / 23.97x vs DuckDB), and claimed_speedup is fixed accordingly. The paper carries a PVLDB 19(11) header, but I did not confirm publication. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 50 stars, archived, last commit 2026-07-22; the artifacts repo has 7 stars.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The paper (arXiv 2603.02081, §4.1) states 2x Intel Xeon Gold 5218 CPUs with 384 GB RAM. The public harness benchmarks/benchmark.py and benchmarks/lib/runners.py (duckdb_benchmark, plus Umbra, ClickHouse, MonetDB and PostgreSQL runners) runs against DuckDB. Generated code is compiled with g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 -fopenmp (src/gendb/orchestrator.mjs).

corrections.claimed_speedup: TPC-H SF10 (Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18): GenDB 214 ms total vs DuckDB 594 ms and Umbra 590 ms (2.8x), and 11.2x vs ClickHouse. Q9 runs in 38 ms, 6.1x faster than DuckDB. SEC-EDGAR (6 queries): 328 ms, 5.0x vs DuckDB and 3.9x vs Umbra. The 163x figure (TPC-H Q18, 12,147 ms to 74 ms) and the 13.3x / 12.7x figures (SEC-EDGAR Q4 / Q6) are GenDB's own gains between optimization iterations, not speedups over a baseline.
corrections.workload: TPC-H SF10 representative subset (Q1, Q3, Q6, Q9, Q18) and SEC-EDGAR: 5 GB of 2022-2024 SEC financial-statement data, with 6 queries sampled from 1,000 SQLSmith-generated ones. LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 4.6 in the paper) generate per-query C++ executables. Baselines are DuckDB v1.4.4, Umbra (February 2026), MonetDB v11.55.1, ClickHouse v26.2.1 and PostgreSQL v18.2, measured on hot, in-memory runs.
corrections.hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (2.3 GHz, 32 physical cores total), 384 GB RAM, Ubuntu (stated in paper)
corrections.caveats: This is the authors' own paper (an arXiv preprint) and repo. The code is LLM-generated per query, so results depend on a particular generation run. Only 5 of the 22 TPC-H queries are used, at SF10. The compiler version is unstated. Baselines use their automatically created indexes, and a second variant adds GenDB-generated indexes. The largest multipliers in the paper (163x, 12-13x) are iteration-over-iteration self-improvements, not comparisons with a baseline.

notes: The record garbled the 163x figure. It is Q18 improving from 12,147 ms to 74 ms across GenDB's own iterations, not '594 ms to 74 ms' and not a speedup vs DuckDB. The headline 2.8x vs DuckDB/Umbra is correct, and the README repeats it. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 75 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-06-08 (active).
